strengths: Novel and reasonably well-motivated idea: instead of 2D-3D projection or CLIP/SAM-lifted features, the paper directly exploits native 3D Gaussian Splatting primitive attributes (opacity, scale) for point-level segmentation, addressing the geometry-appearance mismatch problem in a principled way.

Technically sound correspondence mechanism: Mahalanobis-distance-based Gaussian-to-point matching that accounts for anisotropic covariance is a sensible improvement over naive Euclidean nearest-neighbor matching, and is empirically validated (Table 8).

Comprehensive ablations covering module contributions (boundary vs. appearance distillation), correspondence metric/k, and alternative strategies for using Gaussian opacity (raw Gaussians vs. direct point-opacity vs. distillation), which help isolate the source of gains.

Consistent improvements across four datasets (ScanNet v2, ScanNet200, ScanNet++, Matterport3D) under a common backbone (PT v3), with particularly notable gains on geometrically ambiguous classes (e.g., refrigerator +6.0 IoU, shower curtain +7.2 IoU), supported by qualitative visualizations that plausibly explain the mechanism (resolving category confusion and incomplete boundary coverage).

No reliance on 2D image projection, CLIP/SAM features, or language supervision at inference, and the distilled appearance encoder removes the need for Gaussian inputs at test time, keeping inference overhead moderate (Table 9).
weaknesses: Overall quantitative gains are modest and sometimes marginal: +1.4 mIoU over PT v3 on ScanNet v2, +0.8/+0.4 on ScanNet++/Matterport3D, and G2P actually underperforms BFANet on the ScanNet200 hidden test set (35.5 vs 36.0), which weakens the "state-of-the-art" framing.

The pipeline depends on externally available, pre-reconstructed 3D Gaussian scenes (SceneSplat-7K) plus a separate per-dataset self-supervised appearance-encoder pretraining stage (Sonata-based, 400 epochs); the added complexity, extra data requirement, and training cost (only indoor scenes are supported, no outdoor evaluation) are not fully justified against the relatively small mIoU gains, and total end-to-end pipeline cost (GS optimization + encoder pretraining + main training) is not reported.

The core novelty is somewhat incremental: the boundary module reuses BFANet's B-S block off-the-shelf, and the ablation in Table 7 shows that simply appending Gaussian opacity to point features ("Points with Opacity", 77.3 mIoU) already captures most of the benefit versus the full distillation design (77.8 mIoU), suggesting the added architectural complexity of the distillation pathway contributes relatively little.

The claim of operating "without any 2D...supervision" is somewhat overstated, since the Gaussian attributes used (opacity, scale, and their appearance signal) are themselves derived from multi-view RGB image optimization during 3D-GS reconstruction; the appearance information therefore still originates indirectly from 2D photometric supervision, which should be clarified.

No code is currently released ("code will be released soon"), and given the multi-stage pipeline (GS preparation, correspondence matching, boundary pseudo-label extraction, appearance-encoder pretraining, main training with multiple losses/hyperparameters), reproducibility is a non-trivial concern without full implementation details or released assets.

Hyperparameters such as the pruning ratio η, matching radius r, and loss weights λb/λd appear to be manually tuned; limited sensitivity analysis is provided to demonstrate robustness across datasets or scene types.

strengths: The core idea of directly aligning 3D Gaussian Splatting attributes (opacity, scale) with point clouds via Mahalanobis-distance-based correspondence, rather than relying on 2D rendering losses or cross-modal projection, is a reasonable and relatively underexplored direction for point cloud segmentation.

The paper provides a fairly comprehensive experimental suite across four datasets (ScanNet v2, ScanNet200, ScanNet++, Matterport3D) plus a hidden test set submission, which is commendable coverage for validating generalization.

Class-wise analysis (Table 2) and qualitative visualizations (Fig. 4) are well-designed to directly support the paper's central claim about geometrically ambiguous classes (e.g., refrigerators, doors, windows), providing more than just aggregate numbers.

Ablations on the correspondence metric/neighborhood size (Table 8), module contributions (Table 5), and alternative ways of injecting Gaussian appearance (Table 7, raw Gaussians vs. direct opacity vs. distillation) are thoughtful and help isolate design choices.
Efficiency numbers (Table 9) are reported honestly, including the non-trivial training/inference overhead, rather than hidden.
weaknesses: The claim of achieving results 'without any 2D or language supervision' is misleading: the 3D Gaussians used as the appearance source are themselves optimized from posed multi-view RGB images via photometric/rendering losses (as acknowledged when discussing SceneSplat-7K reconstructions). The appearance signal distilled into the point encoder therefore originates from 2D image supervision indirectly, so the framing as a purely native-3D, 2D-supervision-free method appears to overstate the contribution and should be corrected or substantially qualified.

The overall performance gains are modest relative to the added system complexity: +1.4 mIoU over PT v3 and +1.1 over BFANet on ScanNet v2, and only +0.8/+0.4 mIoU on ScanNet++/Matterport3D, while requiring an entirely separate per-scene Gaussian Splatting reconstruction pipeline, a self-supervised appearance-encoder pretraining stage (Sonata-based, 400 epochs per dataset), and additional distillation losses.

On the ScanNet200 hidden test set (Table 4), G2P actually underperforms BFANet (35.5 vs 36.0 mIoU) and is only on par for Head classes, which weakens the paper's central narrative of consistent superiority and is not adequately discussed or reconciled with the validation-set results.

The method's boundary-guidance component directly reuses BFANet's boundary-semantic (B-S) block; the novel contribution is essentially substituting BFANet's boundary labels with Gaussian-scale-derived pseudo-labels merged via OR with semantic boundaries. The ablation in Table 5 does not clearly disentangle how much benefit comes from the borrowed B-S architecture itself versus the proposed Gaussian-based boundary pseudo-labels, making the incremental algorithmic contribution harder to assess.

The method's applicability is fundamentally gated on the availability of pre-reconstructed, per-scene 3D Gaussian representations (via SceneSplat-7K), which is a heavy, non-trivial preprocessing requirement (per-scene optimization, ~1.5M Gaussians/scene) that is not available for outdoor scenes or many other benchmarks, and no timing/cost analysis of this preprocessing step is reported, understating the true practical overhead of the pipeline.

Reproducibility is currently unverifiable since code is not yet released ('Code will be released soon'), and several implementation details (e.g., sensitivity of the pruning ratio η=0.7, robustness of the Mahalanobis correspondence radius r across scenes of different density) are not thoroughly analyzed beyond a single dataset's ablation.

The paper's framing around 'geometric bias' and appearance cues, while intuitive, is empirically supported mainly through hand-picked qualitative examples (Fig. 4) and a post-hoc class grouping (Table 2) chosen by the authors themselves as 'geometrically challenging,' which somewhat limits the objectivity of the claimed diagnosis versus a more principled boundary/ambiguity metric.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important limitation of point cloud segmentation: geometric bias for appearance-distinguishable but geometrically similar objects (e.g., coplanar doors/windows/refrigerators).

The core idea of transferring 3D Gaussian Splatting attributes (opacity, scale) directly to point clouds in native 3D space, rather than through 2D-3D projection, is a novel and reasonable way to sidestep cross-modal misalignment issues that plague prior 2D-3D fusion methods.

Technically sound alignment procedure: using Mahalanobis distance (accounting for Gaussian anisotropy) rather than naive Euclidean distance for point-Gaussian correspondence is well justified and empirically validated (Table 8).

The distillation-based design (pretrained appearance encoder distilled into the segmentation network) is a sensible engineering choice that avoids requiring Gaussian attributes at inference time, improving practical deployability (Table 7, Table 9).
Comprehensive experimental validation across four benchmarks (ScanNet v2, ScanNet200, ScanNet++, Matterport3D) with consistent, if modest, improvements over strong baselines (PT v3, BFANet).

Thoughtful class-wise analysis (Table 2) and qualitative figures (Fig. 4) that directly support the paper's central claim by showing gains concentrated on geometrically ambiguous classes (refrigerator, shower curtain, door, window).
Reasonably thorough ablations isolating the contribution of boundary guidance vs. appearance distillation, and correspondence hyperparameters (k, distance metric).
weaknesses: Overall quantitative gains are modest (+1.1–1.4 mIoU over BFANet/PT v3 on ScanNet v2, +2.1 on ScanNet200), and on the ScanNet200 hidden test set G2P actually underperforms BFANet (35.5 vs 36.0 mIoU), tempering the 'state-of-the-art' claim in the conclusion.

The method fundamentally depends on the availability of a pre-optimized, per-scene 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstruction (via SceneSplat-7K), which is a nontrivial preprocessing/data requirement not shared by pure point-based baselines; the paper does not discuss the cost, robustness, or sensitivity of results to the quality of the underlying GS reconstruction.

The approach appears restricted to indoor benchmark scenes for which curated GS reconstructions exist; the paper explicitly notes outdoor scenes are unavailable in SceneSplat-7K, limiting demonstrated generality and leaving open whether GS reconstruction is even practical/reliable for other domains (e.g., outdoor LiDAR, sparse scans).

Training overhead is substantial (training latency +67%, memory +30%; inference memory +74%), which is a real deployment cost that is somewhat downplayed in the conclusion’s framing of 'moderate' inference overhead.

In the appearance-transfer ablation (Table 7), the gain from full distillation (77.8) over simply concatenating opacity directly as a point feature (77.3) is small (+0.5 mIoU), raising a question about whether the added complexity of the appearance-encoder pretraining and distillation pipeline is fully justified versus a simpler baseline.
No code, pretrained weights, or released Gaussian correspondences are currently available (code 'to be released'), limiting immediate reproducibility.

The paper does not report variance across seeds/runs, making it hard to assess whether the reported mIoU gains (often ~1 point) are statistically meaningful versus run-to-run noise typical in these benchmarks.

Limited discussion of failure cases or scenarios where GS-derived attributes might be noisy, incorrect, or unhelpful (e.g., poorly reconstructed thin/reflective/transparent regions, which are exactly the challenging classes targeted), which would strengthen the paper's honesty about limitations.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated approach that transfers 3D Gaussian Splatting attributes (opacity, scale) to point clouds through explicit point-wise correspondence, avoiding the pixel-alignment and occlusion issues that plague 2D-3D fusion methods.

Clear engineering design: keeps input geometry as raw points (avoiding GS structural drift issues) while using GS attributes only as auxiliary distillation/boundary signals, and achieves Gaussian-free inference, which is practically attractive.

Extensive experimental validation across four benchmarks (ScanNet v2, ScanNet200, ScanNet++, Matterport3D) plus instance segmentation, with consistent (if modest) improvements over the PT v3 baseline.

Thorough ablation studies (Mahalanobis vs Euclidean matching, k neighbors, loss weight sensitivity, boundary pseudo-label source, attribute choice for distillation vs direct input) that support the specific design decisions.

Useful supplementary analysis (attribute distribution visualization, PCA of learned features, PSNR-mIoU correlation) that provides some interpretability regarding why scale/opacity are informative and clarifies that improvements are not merely due to reconstruction fidelity.

Class-wise analysis convincingly demonstrates that gains are concentrated on the intended target: geometrically ambiguous but appearance-distinctive classes (e.g., refrigerator +6.0 IoU, shower curtain +7.2 IoU), supporting the core motivating claim of the paper.
Honest discussion of limitations (offline dependency on Gaussian reconstruction, outdoor-scene applicability) rather than overclaiming general applicability.
weaknesses: Overall quantitative improvements are fairly modest (e.g., +0.4 mIoU over BFANet, +0.9 over PT v3 on ScanNet v2; on the ScanNet200 hidden test set G2P actually underperforms BFANet, 35.7 vs 36.0 mIoU), raising questions about the practical significance of the gains relative to added complexity and cost.

The method depends on a costly offline pipeline (GS optimization ~22 min/scene, appearance-encoder pretraining ~28h/dataset) and on externally provided GS reconstructions (SceneSplat-7K), which limits reproducibility/generality and is a substantial practical overhead not fully reflected in the main comparisons of mIoU vs. baselines.

Training overhead is non-trivial (+67% latency, +30% memory) and inference overhead is also non-negligible (+21% latency, +74% memory), which somewhat undercuts the claimed practicality of a 'Gaussian-free inference' design.

The technical contribution is largely a combination of existing components (Sonata-based distillation, BFANet's boundary-semantic block, Mahalanobis-based attribute aggregation) rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea; novelty lies mainly in the specific application of GS attributes to point segmentation.

Comparisons to prior 2D-3D fusion or Gaussian-based segmentation baselines are somewhat narrow (mainly UniPre3D), and the paper does not compare against other plausible Gaussian-informed segmentation baselines with similar computational budgets.

The reliance on outdoor-scene inapplicability and dependency on high-quality GS reconstructions (with some sensitivity noted for low-PSNR scenes) constrains the scope of claimed impact to indoor, well-reconstructed scenes only.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated problem (appearance-geometry ambiguity in sparse point clouds) and proposes a reasonably principled way to transfer 3DGS attributes to points while preserving original point geometry, avoiding the projection/occlusion issues of 2D-3D fusion.
The Mahalanobis-distance-based Gaussian-to-Point matching that accounts for Gaussian anisotropy is a sensible design choice, and the ablation (Tab. 10) shows it outperforms naive Euclidean matching.

Extensive experimentation across four datasets (ScanNet v2, ScanNet200, ScanNet++, Matterport3D), plus instance segmentation and efficiency analysis, together with a large number of ablations (attribute choice, distillation vs. direct input, loss weights, pruning ratio, boundary label source) that substantively probe the design space.

Class-wise analysis and qualitative figures convincingly illustrate the intended failure mode (coplanar/reflective objects) and show visually improved segmentation for hard categories such as refrigerator and shower curtain.

Reasonable transparency about limitations (offline GS dependency, outdoor scene limitations) and a supplementary analysis of what Gaussian attributes actually encode (scale vs. opacity vs. rotation vs. SH).
weaknesses: The headline quantitative gains are marginal and inconsistent: only +0.9 mIoU over PT v3 and +0.4 over BFANet on ScanNet v2, +0.6 mAP over PT v3 on ScanNet200 instance segmentation (mAP 23.1→23.2), and the method actually underperforms BFANet on the ScanNet200 hidden test set (35.7 vs 36.0 mIoU). No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported, making it hard to judge whether these small deltas are meaningful.

The method depends on pre-existing, high-quality offline 3D Gaussian reconstructions (SceneSplat-7K, ~1.5M Gaussians/scene, ~22 min/scene optimization) and a per-dataset teacher pretraining stage (27.9 GPU-hours/dataset). This is a heavy, non-trivial pipeline for the reported gains, and the method is explicitly inapplicable to outdoor or scenes without existing GS reconstructions, substantially limiting practical impact and reproducibility for typical point-cloud-only settings.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core contributions largely recombine existing components (Mahalanobis neighbor aggregation, the BFANet boundary-semantic block used verbatim, Sonata used as a distillation teacher, standard CE/Lovász/Dice losses). The technical delta over BFANet + a feature-distillation branch is relatively small.

Some ablations reveal fragility: directly fine-tuning the appearance encoder with GS-derived attributes (Tab. 9) yields mIoU (74.9-75.0) below the plain PT v3 baseline (77.0), indicating naive use of the proposed attributes can hurt performance and that the benefit is contingent on a specific distillation recipe rather than a robust general finding.

The correlation analysis between GS reconstruction quality (PSNR) and downstream mIoU (Fig. 10) shows essentially no correlation, which is presented as a strength ("robustness") but could equally suggest the transferred Gaussian attributes carry weak or noisy signal, undermining the core causal claim that opacity/scale specifically drive the improvements.

No comparison against simpler, GS-free alternatives that could plausibly capture similar cues (e.g., local curvature/normal-variation-based boundary pseudo-labels, or simple point density/confidence proxies), so it is not fully established that 3DGS is necessary to obtain these gains versus cheaper geometric heuristics.

Training overhead is non-trivial (+67% training latency, +30% training memory) for the achieved gains, and while inference overhead is smaller, the overall cost-benefit trade-off is not strongly favorable given the marginal accuracy improvements.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and clearly articulated problem: geometry-only point cloud representations struggle to disambiguate objects with similar shape but distinct appearance (e.g., coplanar doors/windows, reflective refrigerators). The framing via 'geometric bias' is intuitive and supported by qualitative failure cases in Fig. 1 and Fig. 5.

The core idea of using 3D Gaussian Splatting attributes (opacity, scale) as auxiliary point features, rather than the noisy Gaussian geometry itself, is a sensible design choice that avoids the structural mismatch problem of directly using optimized Gaussian positions, and it differentiates the work from prior 2D-3D fusion pipelines that suffer from projection/occlusion artifacts.

The Mahalanobis-distance-based Gaussian-to-Point correspondence, which accounts for Gaussian anisotropy, is a reasonable and empirically validated technical contribution (Tab. 10, Fig. 7) over naive Euclidean matching.

Extensive empirical validation across four benchmarks (ScanNet v2, ScanNet200, ScanNet++, Matterport3D), including both semantic and instance segmentation, plus hidden test set evaluation on ScanNet200.

Rich ablation studies covering attribute choice (opacity vs. scale vs. SH vs. rotation), distillation vs. direct input, boundary pseudo-label formulation, loss weight sensitivity, and neighborhood size, which strengthen the credibility of the design choices.

Class-wise analysis (Tab. 3) and qualitative comparisons convincingly show that gains are concentrated on geometrically ambiguous classes (refrigerator +6.0 IoU, shower curtain +7.2 IoU), which is consistent with the paper's central claim and adds interpretability beyond aggregate mIoU numbers.

Thoughtful supplementary analysis (attribute visualization, PCA of encoder features, PSNR-vs-mIoU correlation) provides useful evidence for why opacity and scale (and not rotation/SH) were chosen, improving scientific rigor.

Practical benefit of Gaussian-free inference: once trained, the model does not require Gaussians at test time, keeping the deployment pipeline relatively lightweight despite a costly offline preparation stage.
weaknesses: The overall accuracy gains over strong baselines are modest and, in some cases, not state-of-the-art: +0.9 mIoU over PT v3 and only +0.4 over BFANet on ScanNet v2; on the ScanNet200 hidden test set G2P (35.7 mIoU) actually underperforms BFANet (36.0 mIoU); instance segmentation gains are marginal (+0.1 mAP, +0.1 mAP50). Given the added system complexity, it is not fully clear the benefit justifies the added machinery.

The method depends on pre-computed, per-scene 3D Gaussian reconstructions (SceneSplat-7K) that require ~22 minutes of GS optimization per scene plus a dataset-specific appearance-encoder pretraining stage costing ~28 GPU-hours per dataset (Tab. 13). This is a substantial and somewhat under-discussed practical cost that limits applicability to new/unseen scenes without existing high-quality reconstructions, and arguably functions as a form of external supervision/data not available to baselines being compared without such preprocessing (yet the paper emphasizes 'no external pretraining' as an advantage over PPT/ODIN/PonderV2, which is a slightly inconsistent framing).

No results on outdoor scenes are presented, and the paper acknowledges GS-based reconstruction is currently unreliable there, restricting the scope of the contribution to indoor, GS-reconstructable scenes.

Training overhead is non-trivial (+67% training latency, +30% training memory in Tab. 11) for the reported accuracy gains, and this overhead is on top of the substantial offline preparation cost, which together raises questions about the practicality/scalability of the approach for large-scale or frequently updated scene collections.

The individual technical components (Mahalanobis-weighted feature aggregation, feature distillation, boundary-semantic fusion borrowed from BFANet) are largely combinations/adaptations of existing techniques rather than fundamentally new mechanisms; the novelty is primarily in the specific combination and application to GS-derived attributes rather than in a new algorithmic principle.

No variance/multiple-seed reporting is provided, so it is difficult to assess whether the reported mIoU differences (often <1 point) are statistically meaningful versus training noise, which is a common concern at this margin of improvement.
